taxonomic_note: Kew recognizes var. ashei and var. marilandica; B011 remains species-level.
look_here_first: Look at adult leaf tips with a loupe: 3–5 broad distal lobes should show small AWNS/bristles (red-oak-group trait). Then check the conspicuous tawny-hairy, often 5-angled terminal buds (5–10 mm), glossy mature upper leaves, and dark bark broken into blocks. Do not rely on a 'duck-foot' leaf alone.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Kew/POWO accepts Q. marilandica, lists Texas as native, and recognizes var. ashei and var. marilandica. USDA PLANTS-derived county/native-status data records Q. marilandica as native in Bell County. The same USDA-derived data records it as native in Blanco County. The same USDA-derived data records it as native in Burnet County. Kerr County: Singhurst et al. (2010), Kerr WMA natural flora, specimens JS 10671, LS 4044, LS 4197. Blanco, Burnet and Kerr are all project target counties; Bell remains out-of-zone context.

best_field_traits: deciduous red-oak-group tree, often small to medium sized on poor uplands
leaf strongly obovate/obtrullate, narrow below and broad toward tip
usually 3–5 broad shallow lobes concentrated in distal half
upper surface dark glossy green; lower surface paler and often tawny-pubescent
mature bark nearly black to dark gray, breaking into thick squarish blocks
Leaf blade typically 70–200 mm long and 70–200 mm wide, strongly broader toward the tip; 3–5 broad shallow lobes and 3–10 awns/bristles.
Upper surface mature glossy/glabrous; lower surface scurfy to scattered pubescent, not the densely yellowish glandular + stellate combination typical of post oak.
Terminal buds conic/narrowly ovoid, 5–10 mm long, noticeably 5-angled and tawny-pubescent; twigs about 2–4 mm wide, pubescent to tomentose.
Acorns mature in second year (biennial); turbinate cup about 6–10 mm high × 13–18 mm broad, enclosing about one-third of nut; scales often free/loose at rim.
Very dark mature bark in rectangular/irregular blocks; inner bark orangish (a nonessential feature and not a reason to damage a live tree).
morphology_keys.oak_training: Use leaf architecture plus bark/twig/buds and mature acorn/cupule; never identify an oak from leaf silhouette alone.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Quercus stellata: Post oak is a white-oak-group species with rounded, non-bristle lobes and often a cruciform leaf; blackjack has bristle-tipped lobes and very dark blocky bark. Quercus nigra: Water oak can develop spatulate three-lobed leaves but usually has smaller, thinner leaves and lacks blackjack's thick leathery 'duck-foot' form and blocky black bark. Quercus buckleyi: Texas red oak has deeper pointed sinuses and more classically red-oak lobed leaves; blackjack is broader and more top-heavy with shallow distal lobes.

diagnostic_comparison.where_to_look_first: First inspect terminal lobe bristles; then terminal buds, twig pubescence, abaxial hair type and mature bark; use cups and fruit maturation when present.

pair_specific_tie_breakers.quercus-stellata: Post oak's lobes are typically rounded, WITHOUT the terminal awns; older twigs are thick and densely stellate-hairy, buds small to 4 mm, often with gray scaly bark. Blackjack's much larger tawny 5-angled terminal bud and shiny broad red-oak blade support the bristle evidence.
pair_specific_tie_breakers.quercus-nigra: Water oak has much narrower/spatulate often thinner blades and smaller acorns; both can have three distal lobes, so bark, bud, leaf texture, and habitat are required.

unreliable_alone: Small inconspicuous bristle tips can break off; do not infer white-oak membership just because a torn leaf lacks a bristle.
Do not confuse post oak's thick yellowish stellar hairs with blackjack's variable pubescence.
Both species occur together on dry/poor upland soils, and FNA reports variable overlapping leaf forms and putative hybrids.
diagnostic_comparison.hybrid_guardrail: Possible intermediates; don't force species ID from variable silhouette alone.
